paras: The attempted lynching of Everidge Williams and Walter Brown was an effort by United States soldiers from Fort Leavenworth and a number of citizens to lynch two Black men at their homes in Leavenworth, Kansas, on the night of Sunday, July 12, 1903. Armed police got both men to the police station before the crowd could act, and no one was killed. The soldiers' part drew editorial comment, and the Secretary of War later told a Black editor that the press account was not correct.

According to the Associated Press, Williams and Brown had a row with soldiers at Ninth and Kickapoo streets, and one of them fired a number of shots at a soldier. An earlier cable instead described a street row in which shots were exchanged and several persons were injured, some seriously. The army's later account said two white soldiers had an altercation with the men, "the Negroes being at fault," and that Williams pursued a soldier with a knife.

Soldiers then gathered in large numbers and decided to lynch the two men if they could be found. About twenty-five soldiers and a number of citizens surrounded the men's homes near the old fair grounds, and the dispatch said ropes had been secured and "everything was in readiness for a lynching." Policemen with Winchesters and revolvers arrived and got Brown and Williams away to the police station. The whole police force was busy for over an hour, and several soldiers carrying revolvers were arrested and later released. Stories of "killing by the score" circulated, the Topeka State Journal said, but no death is reported.

Military officers were asked to suspend all passes for soldiers at the fort. The Butte Inter Mountain predicted severe military punishment for the soldiers, but no report of a court-martial appears in the coverage. According to the department commander's report, quoted by Secretary of War Elihu Root on July 24, police arrested Williams and Brown, who were tried the next day and, "having bad reputation," fined twenty-five and fifty dollars. The report called the pursuing crowd "angry, but not unruly" and said police had not thought the affair important enough to notify the post's commanding officer.

The Associated Press story ran on July 13 and 14 from Topeka and St. Paul to Birmingham, Omaha and St. Louis, under headlines such as "Soldiers Attempt to Lynch Blacks" and "Try to Lynch Two Negroes." The New-York Tribune headed it "Soldiers Organize Lynching Bee," and the Chicago Eagle "Soldiers Lead Kansas Mob." Honolulu papers printed the first cable, and digest columns in Texas, Minnesota and South Carolina reduced the story to a line.

Editorial writers drew different lessons: the Butte Inter Mountain wrote that "Uncle Sam does not stand for lawlessness on the part of his soldiers" but that the acts of "these Leavenworth regulars" must not be charged against the army. Southern papers turned the episode against Northern critics: the Wilmington Messenger, quoted in the Richmond Times Dispatch, said it was "time to stop charging lynching as a species of barbarity peculiarly southern," and the Charleston News and Courier, quoted in the Yorkville Enquirer, doubted the regulars' neutrality "in the event of trouble between the races." The New York Post, reprinted in the Kansas Agitator, called the attempt "very ominous" and blamed attitudes the soldiers had acquired in the Philippines.

In the Black press the episode surfaced through the Cleveland Gazette, whose editor, Harry C. Smith, sent a clipping to the War Department on July 16. On August 8 the Gazette printed Root's reply under the headline "Secretary of War Writes And Sends the Truth of the Reported Attempt to Lynch Two Afro-Americans by U. S. Soldiers."

The Associated Press said one of the men fired shots at a soldier, the first cable said shots were exchanged, and the army's report mentioned only a knife. The wire reports said the crowd meant to lynch the men and brought ropes, while the army's report, drawn from the soldiers' own command, called the crowd "not unruly" and mentioned no ropes. No account from Williams or Brown appears in the coverage, and their names vary, the New-York Tribune giving "Eldridge Williams" and the Butte Inter Mountain "Everad Williams and John Brown."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Everidge Williams and Walter Brown
bases: Wire reports say soldiers and citizens surrounded the two men's homes with ropes intending to lynch them before police removed them (A2, A6, A18); the attempt failed and the episode is coded as an attempted lynching, a version the War Department disputed (A31).

No one was killed: police got Williams and Brown to the police station before the crowd of about twenty-five soldiers and citizens could act (A2, A6); the crowd acted without authority in reprisal for an alleged shooting at a soldier (A2), so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

Many wire reprints and a separate first cable agree that a crowd of soldiers threatened to lynch two Black men (A2, A3, A6, A18), but the War Department's report, printed in the Cleveland Gazette, said the crowd was 'angry, but not unruly' and that the press account was not correct (A31).

accounts.label: First cable (July 12)
accounts.gist: Negroes and soldiers had a street row in which shots were exchanged and several persons were injured; soldiers and citizens formed a mob and declared their intention to lynch the negroes; armed police had great difficulty dispersing it.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: After one of the two men fired shots at a soldier, about twenty-five soldiers and some citizens surrounded the men's homes with ropes ready; police with rifles and revolvers got them to the police station; some armed soldiers were arrested and released.

accounts.label: Department commander's report (via Secretary of War)
accounts.gist: Two white soldiers had an altercation with the men, who were at fault; Williams pursued a soldier with a knife; a crowd followed them home but was 'angry, but not unruly'; police arrested the two men, who were tried and fined the next day.

framing.detail: AP story carried widely on July 13-14 under headlines such as 'Soldiers Attempt to Lynch Blacks' and 'Try to Lynch Two Negroes', presenting the men's alleged shooting as the cause.
Butte Inter Mountain editorial 'Case for Army Discipline' predicted severe military punishment but said the acts of 'these Leavenworth regulars' must not be charged to the army.

Southern papers (Wilmington Messenger via Richmond Times Dispatch; News and Courier via Yorkville Enquirer) used the soldiers' attempt to rebut the charge that lynching was peculiarly southern and to question regular soldiers' sympathies in racial conflict.
New York Post comment, reprinted in the Kansas Agitator, called the attempt 'very ominous' and blamed attitudes learned in the Philippines.

Cleveland Gazette printed the Secretary of War's letter under 'Secretary of War Writes And Sends the Truth of the Reported Attempt to Lynch Two Afro-Americans by U. S. Soldiers', without recorded comment.
